title: The First Beautiful Error
memory_text: The green vessel made Lenz proud of his craft, and I disliked spoiling his satisfaction with an unsatisfactory occupant. A pale little crescent had appeared against the glass, exquisite in outline, quite without a blemish visible to the lens. Beside it, in a crooked vessel Clara had brought, another growth showed a disagreeable swelling. I displayed the crescent to a visiting naturalist and put the crooked specimen beneath the bench. Within the week the crescent had stopped altogether. The swollen specimen continued its obscure business. Clara placed both vessels on my table without a word, which was an intolerable form of criticism. I entered the results under separate headings, Beauty and Continuance. Lenz asked why I had not merely written Success and Failure. Because, I explained, I had yet to decide which result deserved which word. I turned the beautiful vessel toward the wall when he left.

observations: The prettiest culture ceased developing before the uneven one
decisions: I retained both and concealed the ugly vessel from a visitor
consequences: The comparison made appearance an enduring source of error
belief_changes: I began keeping beauty and viability in separate columns
relationship_changes: Lenz noticed that I preferred the glass he had tinted

title: The Gentleman Who Paid for a Face
memory_text: A collector sent two coins and requested a drawing of the finished creature I had mentioned, most injudiciously, over supper. There was no finished creature. There was a diagram of a symmetrical head that had never possessed more than the possibility of one. Friedrich Behr, who could turn my atrocious ink into legible type, suggested putting the word proposal beneath the sketch. The collector removed it in his imagination and congratulated me upon an achievement. I accepted the payment for the drawing and returned his request to see the living specimen. Afterward I spent three nights trying to make the next trial resemble the charcoal outline. Behr observed that I had allowed a gentleman's purse to become an anatomical authority. I told her the purse had purchased precisely the opposite privilege, namely the right to be disappointed later. I did not return the coins. We needed glass more urgently than we needed spotless consciences.

observations: A collector valued the drawing more than its failed subject
decisions: I sold a sketch but refused to sell the specimen
consequences: Money funded new glass while vanity warped the next trial
belief_changes: Praise for appearances was not evidence for vitality

title: A Vessel without a Witness
memory_text: Henry found me watching a minute fleck rise each time I tapped the glass. I called it anticipation. He asked whether it rose when I did not tap. A particularly tiresome question, since no one had proposed holding a séance for a bit of tissue. He folded a card around the side of the vessel, moved the tapping point and found that the fleck no longer rose. He had removed a current I had overlooked. I informed him that invalidating my interpretation did not invalidate the observation, and he agreed, smiling in a way that suggested he had expected a battle. We spent the rest of the afternoon making marks on cork and moving a watch from one end of the bench to the other. When he departed I wrote his suggestion in my ledger. I did not write that he had been pleased to have caught me. That would have made the record unnecessarily human.
prior_expectations: A single observer could recognize genuine advance
observations: Henry found my favored response disappeared when the vessel was rotated
decisions: I repeated the trial in his presence and refused to call the first result fraud
consequences: We began arguing over what counts as independent observation
belief_changes: An unwelcome control may be the only useful result
relationship_changes: Henry acquired permission to challenge my demonstrations

title: The Little Arm That Wasn't
memory_text: For eleven days I drew a splendid little arm, bent at the elbow, terminating in what might almost have been a hand. I drew it from the same place at the same hour, with the lamp to my left. Lenz arrived carrying a repaired stopper and, without consulting my scientific dignity, lifted the vessel onto a felt pad. The arm vanished. He rotated it once more and showed me an innocent membrane, folded by a distortion in his own curved glass. I called the workmanship criminal. He asked whether I should prefer the glassblower to have manufactured the limb itself. The replacement vessel had one flat wall, an atrocity to look upon and a great improvement to the eye. I kept the old sketches. When I saw the handsome false arm again, I remembered not how I had been deceived but how very quickly I had wished to be.

observations: The supposed limb was a fold seen through curved glass
decisions: I paid Lenz to remake the vessel with an inelegant flat wall
consequences: Weeks of confident sketches became a warning against optics
belief_changes: I grew suspicious of perfect outlines under perfect light
relationship_changes: Lenz gained unusual freedom to criticize my apparatus

title: The Dullest Sunday
memory_text: I had been in the laboratory since Saturday, troubling a stubborn vessel with inspections that produced nothing but a sore neck. At nine the church bells began. I was tempted to declare the entire culture dead and salvage my Sunday by declaring an enemy defeated. Clara called to fetch me for an inventory of ordinary medicines. I followed her because the lamp oil had run out and because she offered coffee without discussing my theories. We counted bottles, argued about a missing label, and ate hard bread with cheese. When I returned at dusk the vessel was precisely as it had been. I was absurdly gratified by this evidence that the world could continue to resist me without requiring my constant supervision. On Monday it moved. I would have preferred it to do so while I was watching, naturally.

observations: The most promising material showed no new activity despite constant handling
decisions: I left it undisturbed and spent the morning with Clara's inventory
consequences: Progress followed no timetable I could command
belief_changes: Interference could be a form of impatience rather than care
relationship_changes: Clara saw me capable of leaving a specimen alone briefly

title: A Face Too Complete
memory_text: The little figure now possessed the beginnings of a face. One side was finer than the other, and I wasted a morning attempting to view the discrepancy as a trick of reflected light. Henry considered its response to an approaching shadow more important than the uneven jaw. Clara asked whether I intended to accuse it of bad breeding. I found both remarks provincial. Nevertheless I abandoned the drawing with its invented symmetry and sat beside the vessel until the shadows lengthened. When I approached with a silver mirror the creature turned away from the brightest patch. If it could choose its comfort over my preferred view, it had advanced beyond any portrait I might devise. I did not describe the episode in these sentimental terms to Henry. I merely forbade him to touch the lamp.
prior_expectations: The first responsive figure should be perfected before presentation
observations: The developing features were uneven though responses remained coherent
decisions: I withheld the drawing and continued watching rather than correcting the asymmetry
consequences: My impatience gave way to a reluctant interval of observation
belief_changes: A living expression could exceed its measured proportions
relationship_changes: Henry attended with care; Clara disliked my word defect

title: Velvet Does Not Make a Sovereign
memory_text: Leonie brought a remnant of violet velvet from a theatre costume. I cut a seat for the Queen and had it fitted beneath her favored ledge. The little monarch approached, placed one hand upon the cloth and retreated with unmistakable dispatch. I blamed the dye. Clara blamed my conceit. Leonie, who had pinned costumes onto living performers for years, suggested that the nap scratched. I touched it with my finger and felt nothing. She put the smallest splinter of thread against the sensitive skin of my wrist. I felt it perfectly then. We replaced the velvet with a plain strip of polished wood and the Queen returned. I kept the scrap in an envelope labelled REGALIA REJECTED. It amused me to imagine a monarch whose taste could not be bought, even with fabric of a most expensive shade.

observations: The Queen preferred an undecorated ledge and avoided the theatrical velvet
decisions: I removed the cloth but kept a tiny embroidered scrap
consequences: I learned decoration could be offensive to its intended subject
belief_changes: Taste could belong to the creation rather than to the creator

title: The King's Nose
memory_text: I compared the King's face with an engraving of Henry VIII, then with a wax bust borrowed from a collector whose trust in my scholarship deserved a better fate. From the left, the resemblance was delicious. From the right, he might have been a provincial tax official with a very small grievance. Henry said I had chosen the Tudor king because my miniature already disapproved of being contradicted. Lenz proposed that we rotate the engraving until history behaved. I laughed more than the joke warranted, then measured the profile again. The numbers refused my preferred comparison. In the ledger I wrote that the resemblance was evocative, not diagnostic. At dinner I told the story as though the King himself had selected the model. Scholars must sometimes be permitted a little poetic licence after correcting their own diagrams.

observations: The King did not resemble the bust from every angle
decisions: I retained the nickname while rejecting the measurement
consequences: The resemblance became a joke and an object of public myth

title: The Archbishop's Unanswered Prayer
memory_text: I set a minute altar near the Archbishop's chamber, an exquisite piece of folded paper, and rang a silver bell while he stood before it. He did not bow. He did not cross himself. He went very still when the bell sounded, and afterward moved toward the place from which the vibration came. I said he was attending to a summons. Clara asked whose summons, God's or mine. I told her those were not invariably distinct in a laboratory. She declined to laugh. We altered the interval of the sound and moved the altar, which remained of no interest whatever. I entered his response under SOUND, not DEVOTION. The little altar stayed on a shelf for months. Its uselessness offended me, because the folds were more elegant than the majority of churches I knew.

observations: The Archbishop responded consistently to the bell but ignored the little altar
decisions: I removed the altar and varied the bell's timing
consequences: The distinction between response and interpretation grew harder to ignore

title: The Devil's Reflection
memory_text: The Devil came to his little cape by means of Leonie's sewing, not infernal providence. She insisted that the shoulders must fall correctly if the garment was to be seen through glass. I held a polished spoon beside my own face and challenged Henry to name the likeness. He said the creature seemed less inclined than I to interrupt a companion. I found this unscientific, and may have been less gracious about the observation than my confidence deserved. The little gentleman paused before his reflection, examined it and walked away. Leonie suggested he had better things to do than admire his own face. I put the spoon in a drawer and explained that its curvature rendered it useless as an instrument. I used it thereafter to stir my gin, where inaccuracies of proportion were rather welcome.

observations: Visitors disagreed over which features constituted the likeness
decisions: I permitted the cape but refused to label the face
consequences: The creature became a private joke that sometimes irritated me

title: The Ballerina Refuses an Encore
memory_text: I had arranged for the Ballerina's favored music to be played three times to impress a private guest. She danced through the first rendition, paused before the conclusion of the second, and refused altogether to respond to the third. I blamed the pianist, who was not present. Leonie played the melody softly once more after an hour of silence, and the tiny dancer raised one arm before sitting down. Leonie asked what would happen to a human dancer obliged to repeat the same figure without rest until an audience was persuaded of its existence. I said we were discussing a creation, not a theatre contract. Yet I sent my guest away and shortened the subsequent sessions. I still liked an encore. I found I liked it better when it was offered rather than exacted.

observations: The Ballerina stopped at a familiar passage and resumed only after quiet
decisions: I dismissed the small audience and shortened the session
consequences: Performance ceased to be a reliable synonym for health

title: The Cabinet of Flawless Things
memory_text: Reuter found a drawer lined in blue felt. It contained the things I had spared the wastebasket because they were handsome: a transparent shell, a minute symmetrical form that had never responded, and a delicate branching structure that suggested intelligence only if one wished it. He asked where I had put their dates and controls. I was furious at the implication that beauty had no probative force. Then I discovered I could not remember which of two nearly identical specimens had been kept warm. I took my pen and labelled the drawer AESTHETIC, NOT EVIDENCE, before he could do it for me. He looked disappointed rather than triumphant. We closed the drawer. It remains the only collection in my laboratory for which I refuse to manufacture a scientific justification.

observations: Reuter found my best-preserved specimens lacked usable experimental records
decisions: I marked the drawer AESTHETIC, NOT EVIDENCE
consequences: A secret display acquired its own rules
belief_changes: Collecting evidence and collecting beauty are different occupations
relationship_changes: Reuter became less willing to accept my demonstrations without books

title: The List I Did Not Submit
memory_text: While the faculty prepared its questions I made an inventory of every instrument, culture, invoice and living vessel in my care. It grew into an indictment of the institution, including the names of men and women whose labor had permitted my work. Lenz delivered a broken clamp and warned that an inquiry could travel along a receipt as easily as an accusation. Clara said that my witnesses had not all volunteered to become defendants. I drew a line through several suppliers and removed the pages concerning arrangements never approved by any committee. Whether this was loyalty, vanity or simple prudence depends upon who tells the story. I placed the full inventory in a sealed envelope. My shorter reply did not save my chair. It did not condemn everyone who had sat near it either.

observations: The same list might expose assistants and confidential suppliers
decisions: I submitted an abbreviated list with crucial procedures withheld
consequences: The hearing remained partly opaque even to later correspondents
belief_changes: Public vindication was not worth every private name
relationship_changes: Clara understood the omission but questioned my motives

title: A Number Removed
memory_text: Reuter found an arithmetic error in my summary of survival intervals, and a particularly cruel one, for it improved the apparent outcome precisely where the committee wished to see it. I could have corrected the working papers quietly, leaving the summary untouched. Instead I took a knife to the number and rewrote the page. Clara, waiting in the corridor, said that no one on the committee would have checked it. I replied that I might have. This was not a declaration of virtue. I was furious that an error of my own had provided the institution with an argument it did not deserve. The new figure made no difference to the verdict. I still remember the scraping of the knife and the clock that continued ticking while I debated whether a single honest number could cost a man his laboratory.

observations: The central survival estimate failed Reuter's arithmetic check
decisions: I revised the number before the next faculty statement
consequences: The corrected result looked less spectacular and remained unpersuasive

title: The One Vessel Left Behind
memory_text: There was room for one more vessel in the wagon. I had to choose between an inactive specimen in an exceptionally handsome bowl and the crate of spare stoppers Lenz insisted we would need before the winter. I chose the stoppers and announced the decision as a triumph of reason over attachment. Lenz did not look at me. He tied the crate with wet rope while I returned alone to the annex. On the bench a chalk circle showed where the bowl had stood for months. I copied the label into the blue ledger, although the last observations were several weeks old, and left the vessel where the faculty might take possession of it. I have occasionally imagined someone opening it years afterward. I have no evidence that anyone did. The empty circle was a more exact memory than any speech I prepared for that day.

observations: One inert culture would occupy precious transport space

consequences: Loss remained without a reassuring interpretation

title: A Better Failure in Winter
memory_text: I had reconstructed a promising university trial with every dimension copied from the blue ledger. It failed before the first week ended. Lenz pointed to a fern of ice upon the northern window and asked which page of my ledger mentioned the temperature of a ruined tower. I had entered the measurements of the vessel, the weight of its fittings and the hour of observation, but not the simple fact that my old laboratory was warm. The stopper had contracted and cracked. I blamed him for the glass, although the stopper was of my choosing. We replaced the vessel and repeated the observation with a different result, no more satisfactory but at least intelligible. I preserved the split stopper in the drawer marked WINTER. A foolish name, but it spared me from calling every inconvenience persecution.

observations: The tower's winter altered the behavior of an apparently identical vessel

title: The Unbeautiful Survivor
memory_text: The ugliest thing in the cabinet endured. It was neither human nor even promisingly animal, merely an organized tangle which grew against the glass like a careless signature. Its symmetrical companions had failed long before winter. Clara moved it to the south window and covered the other empty jars with linen. I told her it was an insult to my method. She answered that it appeared to be having an exceptionally good life without consulting my opinion. One evening I caught myself making a drawing of the twisted root with uncommon care, following each detour of its outline. I did not make it beautiful. I made it exact, which gave a pleasure I had not expected. I still would not have shown it to an admirer of my miniature Queen. I was beginning to learn how many audiences I kept inside my own head.

observations: A warped growth outlasted its balanced companions
decisions: I continued observing the unlovely material and refused to exhibit it
consequences: Unwanted survival undermined my ideal of graceful organization
belief_changes: Stability and symmetry were evidently poor relations

title: The Chamber Too Large
memory_text: We spent five days constructing a vessel proportioned for a figure ten times the customary size. I had drawn it beautifully, and had consulted Lenz about every pressure and joint. We had neglected to consult the stairway. The chamber passed through the workshop door and lodged at the turn above the first landing, where it remained like a very expensive coffin. Lenz measured the clear width again while I proposed taking down a section of stone. He refused to work upon the wall without an engineer. In the end we disassembled the apparatus in the rain and carried it upward in pieces, where the rebuilt frame proved less true than before. I entered its cost under INFRASTRUCTURE, an ugly word for an ugly afternoon. I have since measured the route of every apparatus before admiring its dimensions.

observations: The experimental chamber could not pass the tower stair

title: The Queen's False Silence
memory_text: A young physician declared that the Queen had grown dull. She remained motionless for his inspection and moved freely an hour after he had gone. I described her recovery to Clara, who asked whether the creature might be tired of us. Naturally I replied that fatigue had not been established. Still, I moved the clock, dismissed callers, and watched from behind a screen until the afternoon light changed. The Queen climbed her ledge, made an orderly circuit and returned to her customary corner. I had learned a valuable caution and felt very little satisfaction in it. A genius whose proof depends upon a subject appearing on command owns not a discovery but a small theatre with an unreliable performer. I did not entirely abandon the theatre.

title: The Living Specimen and the Silk
memory_text: Mathilde came with a proof of my account of miniature differentiation. I had described a series of splendid appearances, each one supported by precise adjectives and very little troublesome arithmetic. She tapped the passage in which I called two vessels successful, then placed beside it the record showing that both had ceased to respond. I asked whether a printer was now to adjudicate viability. She said a reader would do so if I gave him the opportunity. We worked through a rainy evening replacing my most handsome sentences with measurements and the names of failures. When I saw the result in type it had lost something of my elegance. It had gained the inconvenient property of being a document I could consult without remembering which claims I had embellished. We kept a copy beside the ledger.

title: The Meal in the Crypt
memory_text: Georg found me eating cold chicken beneath the stone ribs of the crypt, with a cigar balanced in the little hollow between two names. He objected to the ash, not to the meal. I moved the cigar and offered him the less respectable half of the bird. He told me about the cemetery wall, which had begun to settle, and the widow who insisted her husband's grave should face her kitchen window. Neither subject involved the soul, death's boundary, or my achievements. I found the conversation restorative. When he left I examined a stain of grease on the cuff of my coat and decided that conventional dining rooms were equally capable of indignity at greater cost. The following Thursday I brought two portions. In my diary I described the arrangement as convenient provisioning.

consequences: Cemetery meals became a comfort that was not solely theatrical

title: The King After the Fall
memory_text: The King had long since survived his fall, yet one stiff movement continued to offend me. I devised a support finer than a spider's bridge and placed it where his gait might be corrected. Reuter watched the little fellow avoid it twice, then saw a fresh mark where the support had caught his limb. He told me to remove it. I demanded a reason better than medical timidity. He showed me the mark and waited. I removed the support. Over the next weeks the King moved more freely, though never with precisely the grace I had intended. I considered this a temporary compromise. Reuter considered it evidence that the creature possessed a body and not merely a design. We were both correct. That did not make his silence during the procedure any less insulting.

consequences: My urge to repair became a danger to a subject I valued

title: The Blind Naming
memory_text: I claimed I could distinguish the promising vessels at a glance. Clara said this was the kind of claim made by men who never allowed anyone to rearrange a shelf. Lenz tied blue ribbons to the lids, marked the bottoms, and asked me to select the soundest specimens while the shutters stood half closed. I chose the most attractive three. Two had already failed. The plain vessel which I passed over continued its obscure growth for another month. I accused Lenz of allowing the light to mislead me. She opened the shutters and invited me to repeat the trial. I did better, though not well enough to justify the original boast. Lenz wrote the scores and showed no particular delight in defeating me. I found her lack of triumph peculiarly difficult to resent.

title: The Garden of Discarded Shapes
memory_text: Clara entered the neglected glass room and found three cultures I had labelled worthless. Their intended shapes had come to nothing. Yet the moss beside one vessel had changed its color, and another had preserved moisture in a place that ordinarily dried by noon. We could not tell which effect belonged to the growth itself and which to my careless storage. I instructed her to discard the whole collection. She asked whether I proposed destroying the observations as well. I kept five vessels and called the result an ecological trial, a term sufficiently grand to conceal that I had been wrong about rubbish. They occupied the west shelf for years. No little man emerged from them, and it would be false to claim they were our finest specimens. They taught me more about the room than any mirror-polished head ever had.

observations: Some discarded forms altered the environment of neighboring vessels
decisions: I preserved a small observation garden but forbade claims of personhood
consequences: Waste acquired a more complicated scientific meaning

title: The Uniform Face
memory_text: Lenz brought a finely graduated gauge and asked why I had copied the same facial proportions into six designs. I said that an intelligent artist does not abandon a solution because it has proved successful. He spread the results on the table: six refined faces, none possessed of the ordinary signs of continued life. The proportions were not the only variable, as he knew, but they were the part I had refused to reconsider. We worked a week altering the drawings. The revised shape offended me and performed no better. I ought to have been pleased that the evidence spared my aesthetic principle. Instead I found myself irritated that the evidence remained insufficient to vindicate anything. Lenz returned the gauge with his name marked discreetly inside the case. I made a note of the inscription and never mistook the instrument for my invention.
prior_expectations: Repeating a favored ratio would repeat its beauty
observations: The same proportion produced lifeless repetition under changed conditions
decisions: I retained the failed plates instead of revising their labels
consequences: My aesthetic rule acquired its first formal exception

title: Seven Years for a Wrong Question
memory_text: Voss helped tie the notebooks of a seven-year series into three bundles. Every book carried some variation of the same idealized profile. I had improved the cheek, corrected the skull, and persuaded myself at least twice that the next vessel would contain the desired result. None had survived long enough to justify the final drawing. Voss asked what question the experiment had been intended to answer. I replied that form could be made to obey the intellect. She pointed out that I had answered a different question, namely how many failures one man would tolerate before improving his records. We ate sour apples while I wrote SERIES CLOSED. I did not write HYPOTHESIS FALSE. The distinction may be vanity, but it is also exact. A failure to obtain proof is not always proof of failure.

observations: Seven years of attempts did not establish the head as the cause of failure

title: An Invoice for Mercy
memory_text: A patron asked to see a figure whose appearance I had described as nearly complete. It possessed an irregular shoulder which no careful lighting would disguise, but its responses remained remarkable. The patron offered to pay for its replacement if I would discard it and show him a prettier version. I informed him that I was not a manufacturer of dolls. After he departed Clara brought me the bill for a sounder vessel, a sum I could ill afford. I paid it by sacrificing a fine wool coat to the second-hand dealer. I was not acting from tenderness, I assured her. The cost of producing a responsive being was simply too great to throw away on account of a shoulder. She asked whether I would give the same answer if the figure were hideous. I told her to bring the invoice rather than philosophy.

title: The Perfect Thing That Choked
memory_text: The chamber was perfect. Its seams vanished beneath a polished rim, its surface held not one visible scratch, and its occupant seemed for a time to sleep in a little palace. Then the signs of distress appeared. Reuter pointed to the airless stillness within the vessel and asked whether I had made a tomb rather than a home. I ordered it opened. The repair spoiled the symmetry of the lid, and a narrow new joint caught the eye like a scar. The creature continued to live. I wrote a full page defending the engineering principles of the earlier seal, and a single sentence recording its replacement. Reuter read both and said nothing. Years afterward I could still see the offending joint before I saw the occupant whose life had made it necessary.

title: The Portrait That Omitted a Scar
memory_text: Mathilde brought a photograph of the chamber whose lid we had altered. The printer had removed the awkward joint, producing a magnificent object that no longer existed. For several minutes I preferred the corrected likeness to the original. Lenz asked why the vessel in the photograph looked cleaner than the one on my shelf. I told him because a photograph was a statement of essentials, not an inventory of scratches. Then I looked again at the absence of the joint and remembered the creature's labored movement. I asked Mathilde to restore the mark before the image circulated. She looked at me as though I had proposed printing a confession. Perhaps I had. I nonetheless made her shift the shadow so that the repair could be seen without making the entire chamber look like an accident.

title: The Failure Dinner
memory_text: I had invited three people to hear a summary of the previous year's experiments, though the summary was chiefly an account of what had not happened. Clara arrived with onions, Reuter with a raincoat he would not remove, and Adler with a bottle he claimed was a more useful contribution than an opinion. I managed to burn the onions while lecturing on the difference between transient and durable responses. Reuter asked whether the subject on my shelf was still living. It was. Then, Clara declared, the year could scarcely be called a total failure. We ate on mismatched green plates and spoke for an hour about an innkeeper none of us liked. Afterward I found the ledger open to its page of disappointments and wrote SUPPER in the margin. It is the only result from that year I have never attempted to replicate precisely.

title: The Equation with a Smudge
memory_text: Mathilde noticed a smudge over one figure in an old table. I had read it as a three. The line beneath suggested an eight. Five subsequent books contained calculations that assumed the first reading was correct. Voss expected an explosion, and I supplied one, directed chiefly at the quill manufacturer and the premature fading of cheap ink. Then we fetched the first notebook. The number was eight. I allowed Mathilde to strike the dependent pages from the active series, though she used a thin rule and blue pencil where I would have preferred dramatic black. For the next week I was unpleasant company. On the eighth day I resumed the experiment from the corrected figures. It remains among the more laborious successes of my career, and produced nothing worth exhibiting.

title: The Little Imperfect Library
memory_text: Mathilde arranged the notebooks on the upper shelf while I dictated what I believed to be a definitive taxonomy of successful experiments. She stopped me at the first category and asked where the books on things which had not succeeded should go. Into the lower cabinet, I said, where they would not encourage visitors. She opened one and found the correction to the smudged calculation that had wasted our winter. We spent the afternoon sorting errors by optical distortion, instrument failure, mistaken response and unfortunate enthusiasm. The titles were appalling. The usefulness was undeniable. I retained my own index of achievements near the desk and gave Mathilde her unlovely library. There are mornings when I consult it before looking at my handsome work. I do not find this an improvement in my temperament.

title: A Journal Named for a Riddle
memory_text: In Munich a bookseller placed a new journal in my hands, its title taken from the creature that asks a question before it offers an answer. Sphinx was much too pleased with its own mystery for my taste, yet its pages included arguments about hypnotism and the soul which no professor of sound reputation would have admitted to reading. I bought the issue and a cheap notebook. Wernig asked whether I believed in spirits. I replied that belief was a lamentably economical substitute for research. In the train I marked claims supported by observations in blue, those supported by admiration for the claimant in red. The latter color soon dominated the page. I nevertheless ordered the next issue. An idea may be badly defended and still point toward a question worth asking.

title: The Dream of the Door in Glass
memory_text: I dreamed of a door set into a wall of clear glass. The handle was on the other side, and behind it stood the Queen, no taller than she was in her chamber, regarding my efforts to reach her without the least alarm. I could have broken the wall, yet in the dream I was terribly concerned that the fragments might injure her. I woke with a cramp in my hand and the odor of a guttering candle in my nose. The drawing I made before breakfast showed a door too narrow even for a child. I labelled it architectural nonsense and shut it inside the blue ledger. It returned months later with different furniture and the same wrong-sided handle. I have never called it prophecy. It was sufficiently irritating as a dream.

title: The Lady of the Blue Curtain
memory_text: Frieda Selke conducted her sittings behind a curtain of faded blue silk. There were orange peels on a saucer and a bell cord within easy reach of a chair. I noted both and expected very little. She declined to summon my father, whose memory would have made a tedious witness, but described a visitor's habit of holding his gloves in one hand. I had never met the visitor. Neither had she, so far as I could establish. The description proved accurate. I felt the violent pleasure of a hypothesis gaining an unexpected ally. I also saw Wernig exchange a folded note with the hostess before we sat down. I returned for another sitting, this time without providing my name. Frieda greeted me as though she had expected precisely that impertinence. I enjoyed her intelligence and distrust equally.

title: The Bell that Answered Twice
memory_text: At the second sitting the little bell answered two questions with exquisite timing. I was considering whether an intelligence had been pleased to hear my voice when Adler pointed out that Frieda's sleeve grazed the cord as she turned. We repeated the motion without questions. The bell sounded. Someone at the table accused us of destroying a sacred atmosphere, as though the atmosphere were the sole witness whose testimony mattered. Frieda's face grew still. She asked whether I had enjoyed the two answers before knowing their source. I confessed that I had, and she said I was therefore no less a customer than anyone else. I paid the agreed fee, declined the third sitting and kept the memory of those two lovely false replies. They were false, not worthless. There is a distinction.

title: Mesmerism without a Master
memory_text: Reuter brought an account of experiments in hypnotism, and we attempted a modest demonstration with an adult volunteer who had agreed to it. Nothing supernatural occurred. The sitter reported heaviness in her arms and a curious alteration in the sound of my voice, though she also admitted she had expected both. When she said she wished to stop, I was on the verge of asking for one more observation. Reuter closed the notebook and stood up. I resented the interruption, because the most interesting sensation had only just begun to be described. The volunteer rose, drank water and went home. I recorded the request and the abrupt ending without removing them from the table of results. It annoyed me that Reuter's decision had been scientifically better than my intention and morally less theatrical.

title: The False Ancient Seal
memory_text: Wernig sold me a folio said to preserve an early alchemical emblem, a figure curled within a closed vessel. It pleased me excessively. I spent a week comparing its circles with the compartments of my own chambers, until Mathilde noticed that the page numbering came from a modern edition. The emblem had been rearranged for a bookseller's plate. I could not prove the publisher's intention, but I could prove it was no untouched survival from an earlier century. I wrote the correction against the purchase price. The design still suggested a way to arrange observations by nested dependencies. I used that suggestion and refused afterward to describe it as ancient wisdom. Wernig offered to take the book back. I kept it, though I ceased to mention its pedigree over supper.

title: A Dream with Three Queens
memory_text: The door returned. On its far side stood three Queens, identical in feature and entirely different in conduct. One knocked upon the glass. One looked away. The third held the handle and would not open it. I woke angry at having been excluded from a room I had apparently constructed myself. Over breakfast Clara remarked that I had spoiled the milk by leaving it too near the stove. Without quite intending to, I told her the dream. She said three creatures might not wish to be treated as one, however they had begun. I accused her of importing philosophy into a damaged night's sleep. She poured fresh milk, which proved wiser than arguing. I drew the three figures separately in the notebook and did not connect the drawing to an experiment until much later.

observations: Three Queens in glass reflected three different fears of replacement
decisions: I told Clara the dream without asking her to interpret it

title: The Unpaid Assistant of the Invisible

She produced one transcript, the record of my own questions, and refused to supply the names of other sitters. I called this unfortunate for science. She said it was fortunate for the people who paid her to be discreet. Then she asked why I had never published the names of everyone who helped me before my dismissal. I found the analogy impertinent and, after consideration, accurate enough to be inconvenient. I paid her for the transcript and left the other questions alone. It was not a conversion to spiritualism. It was an admission that even questionable practitioners may keep an obligation which a respectable man would violate.

title: An Ethical Error without a Violation

The question had little value beyond satisfying my curiosity and proving that I could sustain control. Voss asked what I expected to learn that ordinary observation had not already shown. I began an impressive explanation and found it wanting halfway through. The little figure continued its daily movements while we argued. Finally I instructed Anna to return the chamber to storage. She asked whether she had made an error in its construction. Not at all, I told her. The apparatus was perfect. The question was vulgar. I resented having to distinguish between the two, and the distinction thereafter became one of my less advertised rules.

title: The Face in the Dirty Window
memory_text: I was climbing the eastern stair after midnight when a pale face appeared against the window, seeming to look inward from a height no man could have reached. I stopped with one hand on the latch. When the rain shifted, so did the features. There had been no visitor. Adler, arriving behind me, asked why I had gone so white. I said the stair was cold. He stood with me while we watched the face dissolve into streams of water and the faint reflection of my own lamp. Later I drew the pattern in the same book that held my glass-door dream. I knew perfectly well what I had seen. What troubled me was the interval in which I had not known. I did not give that interval the dignity of a ghost story.

title: The Second Life of a Broken Jar

I was preparing a complaint when Anna observed that the mark fell exactly across the point we had difficulty locating on successive evenings. She used it to align the observations, and the measurements grew more consistent. There was nothing magical in this improvement. The scratch simply remained where the other marks had shifted. I kept the jar and began calling it the honest one. Anna found this description insufferable, though she continued to bring it whenever we discussed that series. Once I caught myself polishing around the scratch so carefully that the glass remained spotless except for the one flaw that had become useful. It was as much a portrait of my temper as any likeness Leonie ever made.

I rescued the useful page and permitted the remainder to wrap a shipment of ordinary paper. When the parcel returned, the torn title had been stained purple with ink. I cut it away and kept the argument in my cabinet, where it joined much less glamorous material on sense and attention. title: The Creature with the Unfashionable Nose

Clara asked whether its behavior was defective. It was not. The creature recognized the approach of a familiar hand, avoided a disagreeable vibration, and returned to its ordinary place when left alone. I had no defensible reason to improve its nose except that I disliked the outline. So I forbade the alteration and had the drawings put away. Adler looked at me with an expression dangerously near satisfaction. I reminded him that ugliness remained ugly regardless of one's moral principles. He agreed and went back to his work. title: What the Rays Could Not Tell Me

title: The Account of a Stranger's Dream

The client did not appear; Frieda gave the account from her notebook, with names concealed. It resembled my dream enough to make me cold, but differed in the position of the door, the company within and even the feeling the dreamer described. I had not told Frieda my earlier dream, so far as I could remember. Yet I had spoken often enough of glass to make accidental resemblance a less heroic explanation than she preferred. title: The Diagram without a Person
memory_text: I spread a large drawing beneath the lamp. Every line was elegant, every joint connected, and every proportion chosen with uncommon care. Anna placed beside it the diary of a living miniature whose odd little habits had survived three alterations of its chamber. The drawing answered what I had intended the being to be. The diary answered what it was doing now. It struck me that an anatomist might admire the first while remaining ignorant of the second. I did not conclude that design was unimportant. Far from it. The design had made the life possible. But the subject had occupied the intervening years with activities I had not specified. I set the diary beside the diagram rather than beneath it and called the arrangement an improvement in filing.

title: A Door Left Unopened
memory_text: Adler asked whether I wanted him to remain for the coming season or whether I would continue scheduling companionship between experiments. I replied with a joke about the reliability of instruments compared with the rest of creation. He did not laugh. We stood at the landing where a brass handle caught the afternoon light, and I recalled, most unhelpfully, the door from my recurring dream. I could have asked him to stay. I could have said that I did not know how much of my work I was prepared to rearrange. Instead I discussed the weather. He went down the stairs and left his gloves on the table, then returned for them without a word. For weeks afterward I worked later into the night than the experiments required. One can call that industry if one does not care to be exact.

title: The Chosen Scar
memory_text: Anna brought the newest chamber and asked whether I wished to hide the repair seam beneath a narrow gilt band. It would have been easy. The chamber was otherwise handsome and its little occupant remained in good health. I held the gold pin against the joint, imagining how the band would complete the line. Voss observed that the seam gave a later observer a reason to ask what had happened. I had not invited her to supply symbolism to an engineering decision. Nevertheless I refused the gilt band. The repair remained exposed, a rough crescent interrupting the polished glass. I could still have made it prettier. I cannot pretend I ceased to want that. I was simply no longer certain that concealment would count as perfection.
